extracted.intended_audience: education researchers, assessment coordinators, and practitioners conducting large-scale student writing assessments
extracted.subtask_description: Protocols and measurement standards for scoring student essays using the 6+1 Trait writing framework (analytic and holistic rubrics), ensuring scorer reliability, managing scoring data, and analyzing results with missing-data procedures and multilevel models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic trait scoring (Ideas, Organization, Voice, Word choice, Sentence fluency, Conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic scoring of student essays using trait-specific scales for Ideas, Organization, Voice, Word choice, Sentence fluency, and Conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report presents variance estimates and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) for each trait when scored analytically. Each trait score is treated separately in multilevel models and in trait-specific impact analyses (tables L1–L6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic rubric scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of holistic rubrics for scoring some cohorts (distinct from analytic trait scoring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICC results are reported for rating teams that used the holistic rubrics (table G3). A common set of essays was used for rater calibration for holistic scoring where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flagging essays with special codes (reasons for unrated essays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Raters applied standard rules for flagging essays with special codes indicating reasons they could not be scored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special codes include: blank or missing data; too short, not in English, or illegible; scored but off topic; and 'no special code'. Raters documented the reason using a special code (table G1). Off-topic essays were scored using regular scoring procedures; essays that could not be scored were documented and excluded from scoring counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rater access and data entry restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissions and limitations for rater system access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rater access was restricted to the data entry screen for the student essay code number, online recording of assessment scores, and entering special code information. Raters could see indicator flags (required scoring, scored once, scored twice) but did not have access to the identity of other raters or the scores assigned by other raters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment coordinator monitoring responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinator-level access to scoring information and monitoring reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinators had access to scoring information entered by raters and real-time project monitoring reports such as number of essays read daily by each rater and for the project, identification numbers of discrepant essays requiring a third read, and the number of times raters changed original scores. The system provided summary tables reporting frequency of discrepant scores and interrater agreement statistics for each rater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrator system privileges
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The online system administrator was the only person allowed to change data entry, storage, and quality-control check functions for the system and had permissions to access all student record numbers, scoring data, and rater information stored in the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rater calibration with a common set of essays
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a randomly selected common set of student essays for all raters to score before analytic scoring sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All participating raters produced independent scores for the common set; these scores were used to calculate ICCs and to assess the extent to which variance was due to essays rather than rater differences. The common set was used for the raters who scored the 2009 cohort using analytic rubrics (not for the second cohort using analytic rubrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrater reliability measured by Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of ICC estimates to determine extent to which variance in scores is related to essays rather than rater differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICC is calculated as [1–rater variance]/total variance and indicates the proportion of total variance in each trait score related to student essay variation. The report considers ICC estimates more accurate than simple correlation statistics. In this project all reliability coefficients were at or above 0.94, meaning 94% or more of variation was due to essays rather than rater differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criteria and handling of 'leavers' for analysis (intent-to-treat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students were included in the analysis only if present at baseline and meeting eligibility; those missing posttest were classified as 'leavers' but included to produce ITT estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leavers (students missing posttest scores) were included in analyses to compute intent-to-treat treatment effects. Analysis of stayers vs leavers assessed differential characteristics (e.g., pretest scores, FRL%, gender, ethnicity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of lowest possible score for blank or too-short essays
rubrics_metrics.description: Students who turned in essays that were too short to score or were blank were assigned the lowest possible pretest or posttest score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 169 students assigned lowest pretest score for too-short/blank pretest essays; 205 assigned low posttest scores for present-but-unscored posttest booklets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple imputation (MI) protocol for missing data
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of multiple imputation when missing outcome data exceeded preset cutoff (5%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MI was implemented with Stata's MI IMPUTE command, imputing remaining missing data on posttreatment assessment and on gender. School ID and recoded ethnicity dummy variables were included as nonmissing variables. Because multiple variables had missing data and no sequential pattern of missingness was observed, imputation assumed multivariate normality. Five sets of complete data were imputed separately for treatment and control groups (10 imputations total), using an iterative Markov chain Monte Carlo method. Proper convergence behavior was checked via trace plots and autocorrelation plots for the worst linear function. The 10 imputed datasets were merged for impact analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear mixed models (LMM) and pooling across imputations
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimation approach for impact and exploratory analyses using imputed datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each MI set was split into paired-school and singleton-school segments; parameter estimation was performed separately for paired and singleton schools by applying LMMs (based on maximum likelihood estimation) to each imputed dataset. The five sets of individual parameter estimates were pooled using inverse-variance weighting (appendix M).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect size standardization (Glass's delta)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardize treatment effect on original scale using control condition standard deviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glass's delta (standardizing by the control group posttest SD) was used because the treatment-effect value on the original scale is difficult to interpret without familiarity with the measurement instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher survey instructional-strategy scales (implementation fidelity measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teacher-reported scales to assess use of classroom practices related to writing instruction (items referencing writing traits sometimes included).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scales (with number of survey items) include: Reading and scoring papers and justifying the scores (5); Teaching focused revision strategies (2); Modeling participation in the writing process (2); Having students read and analyze materials that demonstrate varying writing quality (2); Giving students writing assignments to respond to effective prompts (4); Weaving writing lessons into other subjects (4); Teaching students to set goals and monitor their progress (5); Integrating learning goals for writing into curriculum planning (4); Teaching ways to structure nonfiction writing (4). A separate scale 'teaching the language of rubrics' existed but was dropped when items referencing traits were removed. Scores ranged 0–6; coefficient alphas and mean scale scores are reported in tables I1–I3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative implementation-fidelity analysis excluding trait-referencing items
rubrics_metrics.description: Recalculate teacher survey scales excluding items that referred specifically to writing traits to test sensitivity of implementation-fidelity findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding items that referred to writing traits had no effect at baseline, changed significance on some midyear scales (e.g., 'teaching focused revision strategies' and 'modeling participation'), and had no effect at end-of-year except for the disappearance of the 'teaching the language of rubrics' scale. Treatment group teachers still reported higher levels of use on most remaining scales.
